ox: Incorrect. 0.42 is 2pq, the heterozygotes as a fraction of EVERYONE. The question asks only about people with the dominant phenotype, so the denominator must shrink to 0.91.
Incorrect. 0.49 is p², the homozygous dominant fraction of everyone. It is not the heterozygote share at all.
Incorrect. 0.21 is pq, half of 2pq. It comes from forgetting the 2 in 2pq (a heterozygote can arise two ways: A from mom/a from dad, or the reverse).
Correct. q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Heterozygotes 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42. Dominant phenotype = p² + 2pq = 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91. Heterozygous among them = 0.42/0.91 = 42/91 = 6/13 ≈ 0.46.

p: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the genotype frequencies are p² (dominant homozygotes), 2pq (heterozygotes) and q² (recessive homozygotes), and p + q = 1. You can only SEE the recessive phenotype directly, so start from it: q² is the recessive phenotype frequency.
When a question says 'among people with the dominant phenotype', you must divide by that group's size (p² + 2pq = 1 − q²), not by the whole population.

x1C_114.trap: Answering 0.42 (carriers as a fraction of everyone) when the question asks about carriers among dominant-phenotype people.
x1C_114.eli: Imagine 100 kids and 9 show the rare trait. That tells you q² = 9/100, so q = 3/10. Then you build the rest of the crowd from p = 7/10.
mem: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
Start from the one you can SEE: recessive phenotype = q².
'Among the dominant phenotype' → divide by 1 − q², not by 1.

fm.f: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p = frequency of the dominant allele, q = frequency of the recessive allele, q² = recessive homozygotes, 2pq = heterozygotes, p² = dominant homozygotes
fm.why: We use Hardy–Weinberg because it turns the one frequency we can observe (q²) into every genotype frequency.

x1C_114.sc: Perfect squares do the work: 0.09 = 0.3², so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. No calculator needed.
x1C_114.mn: p² = Pure dominant, 2pq = Pass-along carriers, q² = Quiet recessive (the one you can see).

ox: Correct. Type A blood is Iᴬ Iᴬ or Iᴬ i. Fraction = p² + 2pr = 0.3² + 2 × 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.09 + 0.36 = 0.45.
Incorrect. 0.09 is only the Iᴬ Iᴬ homozygotes. Type A also includes Iᴬ i people, who have the A phenotype because Iᴬ is dominant to i.
Incorrect. 0.36 is only the Iᴬ i heterozygotes (2pr). It leaves out the Iᴬ Iᴬ people, who are also type A.
Incorrect. 0.30 is the ALLELE frequency of Iᴬ, not the frequency of the blood type. People can carry Iᴬ and still be type AB, and the A phenotype also comes from two copies.

concept.t: ABO blood types from allele frequencies
p: Three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i) give six genotypes and four phenotypes. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other, and both are dominant to i. If p, q and r are the frequencies of Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i, then type A = p² + 2pr, type B = q² + 2qr, type AB = 2pq and type O = r².

x1C_087.trap: Counting only Iᴬ Iᴬ (0.09) or confusing the allele frequency 0.3 with the phenotype frequency.
x1C_087.eli: Type A people are everyone who carries at least one A and no B: the AA people plus the A-and-O people.
mem: Type A = IᴬIᴬ + Iᴬi; type B = IᴮIᴮ + Iᴮi; AB = IᴬIᴮ; O = ii.
Type O is the only one you can read straight from an allele: O = r².
Allele frequencies add to 1 (0.3 + 0.1 + 0.6 = 1).

fm.f: Type A = p² + 2pr, where p = frequency of Iᴬ, r = frequency of i, p² = Iᴬ Iᴬ people, 2pr = Iᴬ i people
fm.why: We add both genotypes that give the A phenotype because Iᴬ is dominant over i.

x1C_087.sc: Type A + type O = (p + r)². So type A = (p + r)² − r² = 0.9² − 0.6² = 0.81 − 0.36 = 0.45.
x1C_087.mn: O is 'ii' (needs two recessives), so O = r². Everything else adds the dominant-carrying genotypes.

ox: Wrong. In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate, but the cells were already haploid (n) after meiosis I. Ploidy stays n. This step looks like mitosis. Trap: confusing it with the halving step.
Wrong. S phase copies DNA, so each chromosome has two chromatids. This increases DNA content but does not change the chromosome count.
Wrong. Crossing over swaps pieces of DNA between homologs. This increases genetic variety but does not reduce the number of chromosomes.
Correct. In anaphase I, each homolog (still two chromatids) moves to an opposite pole. Each daughter cell gets only one chromosome of each pair, so 2n becomes n.

concept.t: What halves chromosome number in meiosis
p: A diploid (2n) cell has two copies of each chromosome, called homologs, one from each parent. Meiosis I separates these homologs into different cells. After that, each cell has just one of each pair, so it is haploid (n).
Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids (the two identical copies of one chromosome). That does not change the chromosome number.

d_1C_1.eli: You have two matching shoes in each pair. Meiosis I gives each of two kids one shoe from each pair. Meiosis II just splits each shoe into its two halves.
mem: Meiosis I is reductional: homologs separate, 2n to n
Meiosis II is equational: sister chromatids separate
Crossing over happens in prophase I
d_1C_1.trap: Choosing sister chromatid separation because it is the 'separation' you know from mitosis.
d_1C_1.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Completely linked genes never recombine, which means 0 percent recombination. At 50 cM, recombination is at the maximum.
Correct. A recombination frequency of 50 percent matches the result of independent assortment. So genes 50 cM apart, or farther, behave as if unlinked.
Wrong. Recombination frequency cannot exceed 50 percent because multiple crossovers cancel each other out. Trap: thinking 100 percent is possible.
Wrong. No crossovers would mean complete linkage with 0 percent recombination, the opposite of 50 cM.

p: Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together because they are physically linked. Crossing over can break up the linkage. A centimorgan (cM) is a unit of distance: 1 cM is about 1 percent recombination.

If two genes are far enough apart, crossovers happen so often that half the offspring are recombinant and half are parental. That is exactly what independent assortment gives, so 50 percent is the maximum.

d_1C_11.eli: Flip a coin for each gene: heads means it is passed from grandma, tails from grandpa. Far-apart genes act like two separate coin flips.
mem: 1 cM is about 1 percent recombination
Maximum recombination frequency is 50 percent
50 percent means unlinked
Closer genes mean lower recombination
d_1C_11.trap: Believing recombination can reach 100 percent or that 50 cM means completely linked.
d_1C_11.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Variable expressivity means people who all show the trait have different severity. The first person shows no signs at all, which is a question of whether, not how much.
Wrong. Codominance means both alleles of a gene are fully expressed in a heterozygote, as in AB blood type. It does not explain a missing phenotype.
Wrong. Epistasis is when one gene masks the effect of a different gene. The question does not describe a second gene.
Correct. Penetrance is the percent of people with the genotype who show any phenotype. A carrier with no signs shows incomplete (reduced) penetrance.

p: Penetrance asks: does the person show the trait at all? If only 80 percent of people with the allele show signs, penetrance is 80 percent. That is incomplete penetrance.
Expressivity asks: among people who show the trait, how strong is it? Mild versus severe is variable expressivity.

d_1C_15.eli: Penetrance is whether the light turns on. Expressivity is how bright it shines.
mem: Penetrance: whether the trait appears (yes or no)
Expressivity: how severe it is when it appears
Incomplete penetrance: carrier with no phenotype

r: Does the carrier show the trait at all?

d_1C_15.trap: Mixing up penetrance (whether) and expressivity (how much).

ox: Correct. Mitochondria in the zygote come almost entirely from the egg cytoplasm. A father passes on none, so none of his children inherit his mtDNA mutation.
Wrong. Sons would inherit only if fathers passed on mtDNA. They do not. Trap: treating mtDNA as Y-linked.
Wrong. Daughters would inherit only if fathers passed on mtDNA. They do not, because sperm mitochondria are not passed on.
Wrong. Half would be the expected ratio for a Mendelian trait from one parent. Mitochondrial DNA does not follow Mendelian rules.

p: Mitochondria have their own small circular DNA (mtDNA). At fertilization, the egg supplies nearly all the cytoplasm and mitochondria. Sperm mitochondria are generally not passed to the embryo.
So mtDNA is inherited from the mother only (maternal inheritance). A mother with a mutation can pass it to all of her children, sons and daughters. A father passes none.

d_1C_16.eli: The egg is the whole house; the sperm only delivers the key. The mitochondria are in the house furniture, so they all come from mom.
mem: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal
An affected father passes it to no children
An affected mother may pass it to all children
d_1C_16.trap: Treating mitochondrial inheritance as X-linked or Y-linked. It follows the egg only.
d_1C_16.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. p53 normally halts the cell cycle (using p21) to allow repair, or triggers apoptosis. Without p53, a damaged cell passes the G1/S checkpoint and keeps dividing, passing on mutations.
Wrong. Losing p53 removes the brakes. Cells would not stay stuck in G2. Trap: thinking loss of a checkpoint protein causes more arrest.
Wrong. p53 promotes apoptosis, so losing it means less apoptosis, not more.
Wrong. Telomere length is controlled by telomerase. Losing p53 does not directly change it.

concept.t: p53, the guardian of the genome
p: p53 is a tumor suppressor. When DNA is damaged, p53 turns on p21, which stops the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint so the cell can repair its DNA. If the damage is too great, p53 triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death).
Without functional p53, damaged cells skip this check and continue to divide. Mutations pile up, leading to cancer.

d_1C_17.eli: p53 is a quality inspector on a factory line who stops broken items. Fire the inspector, and broken items just keep going.
mem: p53 is a tumor suppressor
p53 activates p21 to arrest at G1/S
Loss of p53 means damaged cells keep dividing and fewer die
Oncogenes are gain of function; tumor suppressors cause cancer when lost
d_1C_17.trap: Treating p53 like an oncogene that pushes growth. It is a brake, and the problem arises when the brake is lost.
d_1C_17.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. To become F+, the recipient must receive the F factor. In an Hfr cell, the F factor is integrated into the chromosome and is transferred last, so mating usually stops first.
Wrong. Becoming Hfr would require integration of the F factor in the recipient. That does not happen because the F factor typically does not get transferred.
Wrong. The donor transfers only a copy of one strand. It keeps its own chromosome.
Correct. The F factor is integrated and enters last. Mating is usually interrupted before then, so the recipient stays F- but may get part of the donor chromosome, which can recombine into its own.

p: Conjugation is bacterial DNA transfer through a pilus. An F+ cell has a free F plasmid. In an Hfr cell (high frequency of recombination), the F factor is built into the main chromosome.

When an Hfr cell mates with an F- cell, it starts transferring its chromosome with the F factor part entering last. The bridge usually breaks first. The recipient gets some donor genes but not the F factor, so it stays F-.

d_1C_25.eli: Copying a long book page by page by hand while the last page has the 'membership card'. If you get interrupted, you have most of the story but no card.
mem: F+ x F-: both become F+ (plasmid transferred)
Hfr x F-: recipient stays F- but gets donor genes
F factor is transferred last in Hfr, so mating usually stops before it enters

r: Stays F-, gets some donor genes

d_1C_25.trap: Treating Hfr like F+, which actually transfers the plasmid.

ox: Correct. A horse gives 32 chromosomes and a donkey gives 31, so the mule has 63. Horse and donkey chromosomes also differ in structure, so they cannot pair up properly in meiosis. Without pairing, viable sperm or eggs rarely form.
Wrong. Mules have normal sex chromosomes (XX or XY). The trap is thinking sterility means a missing sex chromosome, as in Turner syndrome.
Wrong. Triploid means three full sets (3n). A mule has two sets, one from each parent species, so it is a diploid hybrid. The odd chromosome count tempts you toward triploidy.
Wrong. Mitochondria divide by a separate process and do not control gamete formation by meiosis. The trap is picking a random organelle fact that sounds technical.

p: In meiosis, each chromosome must find its matching partner (its homolog) and pair up. This pairing is called synapsis. If the two sets of chromosomes come from different species, they do not match well.
Horse (64 chromosomes) and donkey (62) cross to make a mule with 63. Chromosomes cannot pair evenly, so meiosis fails and the mule makes almost no working gametes (sperm or eggs).

d_1C_28.eli: Imagine a shoe store where you must match every left shoe with a right shoe. A mule has shoes from two different brands, so many shoes have no match.
mem: Meiosis needs homologous chromosomes to pair (synapsis).
Hybrids of different species are usually sterile because chromosomes cannot pair.
Mule = horse (2n=64) + donkey (2n=62), so 63 chromosomes.
d_1C_28.trap: Do not blame a missing sex chromosome or triploidy. The real problem is failed pairing in meiosis.
d_1C_28.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. In meiosis I, both homologs of the pair go to the same pole. Both daughter cells are abnormal (one has an extra chromosome, one is missing one). Meiosis II then splits each into two, so all four gametes are abnormal: two n+1 and two n-1.
Wrong. Two normal and two abnormal gametes is the result of nondisjunction in meiosis II, where only one of the two cells is affected. The trap is mixing up which division failed.
Wrong. Four normal gametes needs no error. The question says one pair failed to separate.
Wrong. This leaves out the n-1 gametes. The cell that did not receive the pair is missing a chromosome, so n-1 gametes must form. Two n+1 and two normal would not add up.

concept.t: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs II
p: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to separate. In meiosis I, homologous pairs should split apart. If one pair stays together, one cell gets both and the other cell gets none of that chromosome.
Meiosis II then splits sister chromatids in each cell. Both cells were already wrong, so all four gametes are wrong: two with one extra (n+1) and two with one missing (n-1).

d_1C_3.eli: Picture two kids who must each take one of a pair of twins home. If one kid takes both twins, the other gets none. Splitting the twins later cannot fix it.
mem: Meiosis I error: all 4 gametes abnormal (2 n+1, 2 n-1).
Meiosis II error: 2 normal, 1 n+1, 1 n-1.
Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
d_1C_3.trap: Students mix up meiosis I and II. Remember: error in meiosis I ruins all four gametes.
d_1C_3.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. A few birds start a new population. They carry only a small sample of the mainland gene pool, so a rare allele can become common just by chance. This is the founder effect.
Wrong. Gene flow is ongoing movement of alleles between populations by migrants. One colonization event is not continued exchange. The trap is seeing birds move and saying gene flow.
Wrong. Directional selection needs the allele to give a survival or reproductive advantage. The question gives no such advantage, so chance is the cause.

Wrong. A bottleneck is a sudden crash of an existing population from a disaster. Here, a small group starts a new population in a new place. Both involve few individuals, which is why they are confused.

p: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small groups. The founder effect is drift that happens when a few individuals leave and start a new population.
These founders carry only part of the original gene pool. A rare allele may be missing or overrepresented. Its frequency shifts by chance, not because it helps survival.

d_1C_8.eli: If you grab a handful of mixed candy from a big jar, your handful may have lots of a rare flavor just by luck.
mem: Founder effect = new colony started by few individuals.
Bottleneck = existing population shrinks suddenly (disaster).
Both are types of genetic drift: random, not adaptive.
d_1C_8.trap: Founder effect (new place, few colonists) versus bottleneck (same place, population crash).
d_1C_8.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. 16% is q squared, the affected (recessive phenotype) group, not the carriers. The trap is stopping after reading the given number.
Wrong. 24% is p times q (0.6 x 0.4 = 0.24). Carriers are 2pq because the heterozygote can form two ways (Aa or aA), so you must double it.
Correct. q squared = 0.16, so q = 0.4. Then p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6. Carriers = 2pq = 2 x 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.48, or 48%.
Wrong. 36% is p squared (0.6 x 0.6), the homozygous dominant group. The trap is mixing up p squared and 2pq.

p: Hardy-Weinberg describes a population that is not evolving. p is the frequency of the dominant allele and q is the frequency of the recessive allele. They add up: p + q = 1.
Genotypes follow p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1. The recessive phenotype shows only in the aa group (q squared). Carriers are heterozygotes (Aa), which is 2pq.

q11.eli: Think of a bag of red and blue marbles. If you know how many pairs are double blue, you can work backward to figure out how many pairs are one of each color.
mem: p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1.
Recessive phenotype = q^2; carriers = 2pq.
Start from q^2, take the square root to get q.

fm.f: q^2 = frequency of recessive phenotype; q = recessive allele frequency; p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq
fm.why: The recessive phenotype is the only genotype we can identify directly, so we start from it.
fm.nc: 0.16 is 0.4 x 0.4, a known perfect square. 2 x 0.6 x 0.4 = 2 x 0.24 = 0.48.

q11.sc: Memorize that 16% points to q = 0.4 (and p = 0.6). The carrier answer is then 2 x 0.24.
q11.trap: Do not answer with q^2, pq, or p^2. Carriers are 2pq.
q11.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up as tetrads (four chromatids). They swap segments at points called chiasmata. This is crossing over and it creates new allele combinations.
Wrong. By metaphase II, the homologs have already been separated in meiosis I. Only sister chromatids remain, and they are mostly identical. The trap is picking a later meiosis stage.
Wrong. In anaphase I, homologs are pulled apart. Crossing over has already happened before this. The trap is confusing separation with exchange.
Wrong. In mitosis, homologs do not pair with each other, so there is no crossing over. The trap is forgetting that pairing is special to meiosis.

p: Crossing over is the swapping of DNA pieces between homologous chromosomes (the matching pair, one from each parent). It happens in prophase I of meiosis, when the homologs pair up closely as a tetrad.
This shuffles alleles into new combinations on each chromosome. It is one reason children differ from their parents and siblings.

q12.eli: Two decks of cards are lined up side by side and you trade a few cards between them before dealing.
mem: Crossing over occurs in prophase I of meiosis.
Tetrad = paired homologs (4 chromatids).
Mitosis has no homolog pairing.
q12.trap: Do not pick the stage where homologs separate (anaphase I). The swap happens earlier, in prophase I.
q12.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. In a large population, random chance averages out, so allele frequencies stay stable. Large populations resist drift. The trap is thinking more individuals mean more change.
Correct. In a small, isolated group, a few random events (who happens to breed, who dies by chance) can change allele frequencies a lot. Isolation also prevents new alleles from arriving.
Wrong. High gene flow brings alleles in and out, which keeps populations similar and works against drift.
Wrong. Strong directional selection changes allele frequencies by fitness, not by chance. The question asks about drift, which is random.

p: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next. It is caused by chance, like a coin flip, not by advantage.

Small samples vary a lot, so drift is strongest in small populations. Isolation makes it worse because no migrants arrive to restore the old frequencies. Large populations average out the chance events.

q13.eli: Flip a coin 4 times and you may get all heads. Flip it 4,000 times and you will get close to half heads.
mem: Drift is strongest in small populations.
Drift is random; selection is not.
Founder effect and bottleneck are examples of drift.
q13.trap: Do not confuse drift (random) with selection (fitness-based) or gene flow (migration).
q13.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome. Splitting them does not separate an allele pair (the two different versions from each parent). This is the exam trap of mixing up anaphase I and anaphase II.
Wrong. Crossing over shuffles alleles between homologs. It explains linkage and recombination, not segregation.
Wrong. Cytokinesis only splits the cytoplasm into cells. Alleles were already separated before that.
Correct. A gene pair has one allele on each homolog. When homologs are pulled apart in anaphase I, each gamete gets only one allele. That is Mendel's law of segregation.

p: Each person has two alleles (versions) of a gene, one on each homologous chromosome. Mendel's law of segregation says these two alleles separate so each gamete gets just one.
Physically, this happens in anaphase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles. Sister chromatids separate later, in anaphase II, and they carry the same allele.

x1C_002.eli: A pair of mittens is split up, and each kid gets just one.
mem: Segregation = homologs separate in anaphase I.
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
Independent assortment = different chromosome pairs orient randomly in metaphase I.
x1C_002.trap: Anaphase I (homologs) versus anaphase II (sister chromatids). Alleles split in anaphase I.
x1C_002.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Each child has a 1/4 chance of being affected and 3/4 of being unaffected. Exactly one affected can happen two ways, so 2 x (1/4)(3/4) = 6/16 = 3/8.
Wrong. 3/16 counts only one birth order. The affected child could be first or second, so you must double it.
Wrong. 1/4 is the chance for one child. It does not use the two-child setup.
Wrong. This treats affected and unaffected as equally likely. They are not: affected is 1/4, unaffected is 3/4.

p: Two carriers (Aa x Aa) have a 1/4 chance of an affected child (aa) each time. Each child is independent, like a new coin flip.
For two children with exactly one affected, add up all the ways it can happen: affected first then unaffected, or unaffected first then affected. Multiply within each way, then add.

x1C_006.eli: Flip a lopsided coin twice. You want exactly one heads. Heads-tails and tails-heads both count, so you add them.
mem: Carrier x carrier: 1/4 affected, 3/4 unaffected (1/2 carrier).
Independent events: multiply.
Different orders: add.

fm.f: P(exactly one affected) = (number of orders) x P(affected) x P(unaffected)
fm.why: Each child is independent, and there are two orders in which exactly one is affected.
fm.nc: Multiply the fractions across, then reduce 6/16 to 3/8.

x1C_006.trap: Forgetting to count both birth orders gives 3/16.
x1C_006.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. 1/8 comes from using 1/2 for the woman being a carrier. That ignores that she is known to be unaffected, so the probability is 2/3, not 1/2.
Wrong. 1/4 assumes the woman is definitely a carrier. She is only probably one (2/3).

Correct. Her parents must both be carriers (Aa x Aa). Her unaffected status rules out aa, leaving AA, Aa, Aa, so she is a carrier with probability 2/3. Two carriers have an affected child 1/4 of the time. 2/3 x 1/4 = 1/6.
Wrong. 1/12 adds an extra 1/2. The 1/4 already includes each parent passing on the allele.

p: Her brother is affected (aa) and her parents are healthy, so both parents are carriers (Aa). Their children are AA, Aa, Aa, or aa (1/4 each for AA and aa, 1/2 for Aa).
She is unaffected, so aa is ruled out. Of the three remaining possibilities, two are carriers. That makes her carrier probability 2/3.

x1C_008.eli: Three equal boxes are left after one is removed from a set of four. Two of the three hold a prize, so the chance is 2 out of 3.
mem: Unaffected child of two carriers: carrier probability = 2/3.
Carrier x carrier: 1/4 affected.
Multiply independent steps.

fm.f: P(affected child) = P(she is carrier) x P(both pass the allele)
fm.v: P(she is carrier) = 2/3; P(affected from Aa x Aa) = 1/4
fm.why: The child is affected only if she is a carrier and both parents pass on the recessive allele.
fm.nc: Multiply the numerators and denominators, then reduce 2/12 to 1/6.

x1C_008.trap: Using 1/2 for her carrier status (it is 2/3 because aa is excluded).

ox: Wrong. Tightly linked genes sit close together and are inherited together, so they do not assort independently. The trap is forgetting about linkage.
Wrong. Alleles of one gene are on homologous chromosomes and separate from each other (segregation). Independent assortment is about different genes.
Wrong. Being on the X does not matter. Two X-linked genes are on the same chromosome and can be linked.
Correct. Genes on different chromosome pairs line up independently in metaphase I, so any combination of alleles is equally likely in gametes.

p: Mendel's law of independent assortment says alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently. This works because each pair of chromosomes lines up in metaphase I without regard to the other pairs.
If two genes are on the same chromosome and close together, they travel as a unit. That is linkage, and it breaks the law.

x1C_010.eli: Shuffling two separate decks of cards. How one deck lands has no effect on the other.
mem: Independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes (or very far apart).
Linked genes violate independent assortment.
Segregation is about two alleles of one gene.
x1C_010.trap: Mixing up segregation (one gene) with independent assortment (two genes), and ignoring linkage.

ox: Wrong. A diet effect in each fish would not be heritable, and the change happened across generations. Evolution needs inherited variation.
Correct. Bright color helps males attract mates (sexual selection) but also makes them easier for predators to see (natural selection). With few predators, the cost drops, so brighter males win.
Wrong. This is backwards. Predators prefer bright guppies, so more predators select for dull males. Fewer predators lets color rise.
Wrong. Drift is random and can go either way. A steady change in one direction after an environment change points to selection.

p: Sexual selection favors traits that help get mates, such as bright color. Natural selection favors traits that help survive, and bright color can attract predators.
When predators are removed, the survival cost falls. The mating advantage then outweighs it, and bright males become more common over generations.

x1C_148.eli: A loud, flashy peacock tail wins friends but also attracts the fox. Remove the fox, and flashy wins.
mem: Sexual selection vs natural selection can oppose each other
Fewer predators: brighter males favored
Directional, repeatable change suggests selection, not drift
Evolution requires heritable traits

ox: Correct. When hybrids are less fit, selection favors individuals that mate within their own species. That strengthens mating preferences that prevent hybridization.
Wrong. Gene flow is movement of alleles between populations and would blend the species. Here the preferences keep them apart.
Wrong. Hybrid vigor means hybrids are fitter than parents. This question says hybrids have low fitness.
Wrong. Drift is random. The strengthening of preferences is driven by selection against low-fitness hybrids.

p: Two populations may diverge, then meet again. If their hybrids are less fit, individuals that avoid hybrid matings leave more fit offspring.
Over time, prezygotic barriers (those acting before the zygote forms, like mating preferences) get stronger. This process is reinforcement, and it helps finish speciation.

x1C_151.eli: If mixing two recipes makes a bad dish, cooks learn to stick with their own recipes.
mem: Reinforcement: selection strengthens prezygotic isolation
Low-fitness hybrids drive it
Gene flow does the opposite and merges populations
Hybrid vigor = hybrids fitter
x1C_151.trap: Choosing gene flow or hybrid vigor, which are opposite in effect or meaning.

ox: Wrong. The common form has lower feeding success because it is not the rare one. It would shrink, not fix.
Wrong. Selection favors whichever form is currently rare. It does not remove both.
Wrong. As the rare form becomes common, it loses its advantage, so it cannot take over completely.
Correct. This is negative frequency-dependent selection. Whichever form is rare does better, so both forms are pushed toward a stable balance and stay in the population.

p: In frequency-dependent selection, how fit a trait is depends on how common it is. In the negative type, a trait is fit when rare and loses its edge when common.
This keeps multiple forms in a population (balanced polymorphism). Neither form can take over, because success makes it common and then disfavored.

x1C_155.eli: If everyone eats the same lunch, the one kid with a different lunch trades for the best treats. If that spreads, the advantage disappears.
mem: Negative frequency-dependent: rare is favored
Maintains polymorphism near a stable equilibrium
Neither allele fixes
Heterozygote advantage also keeps variation, by a different mechanism
x1C_155.trap: Assuming the currently favored form simply fixes. Its advantage depends on being rare.

ox: Wrong. The question says the allele is neutral, meaning it has no effect on fitness. Do not give it credit for the rise just because it increased.
Wrong. Independent assortment shuffles genes on different chromosomes. Tightly linked genes sit close together and are inherited together, so they do not assort independently.
Wrong. New mutations are rare and slow. They cannot explain a fast rise in frequency that happens alongside a favored allele.
Correct. The two alleles sit close together on the same chromosome, so recombination rarely separates them. When selection pushes the favored allele up, the neutral allele rides along.

p: An allele is one version of a gene. Natural selection pushes helpful alleles to become common. Genes that sit close together on a chromosome are linked, meaning they are usually inherited as one block.
If a neutral allele (one that does nothing helpful or harmful) is linked to a helpful allele, it gets carried up in frequency too. This is called hitchhiking.

x1C_158.eli: Imagine a kid sitting in the back seat of a car going to a party. The kid did not choose the trip, but goes wherever the driver goes.
mem: Hitchhiking = neutral allele rises because it is tightly linked to a favored allele.
Tight linkage means very little recombination between the two.
A selective sweep lowers variation near the selected gene.
x1C_158.trap: Students think any allele that rises in frequency must itself be favored. Here it is neutral; linkage explains the rise.

ox: Correct. Plug in the numbers: 4 x 10 x 90 = 3600, and 10 + 90 = 100, so Ne = 36.
Wrong. 100 is just the head count of breeders (the census size). The formula punishes an uneven sex ratio, so Ne must be smaller than 100.
Wrong. This comes from averaging 10 and 90. The formula multiplies the two numbers instead, so the rarer sex has a huge pull on the answer.
Wrong. This uses 2 x the number of males. The formula needs both sexes in the numerator and the total in the denominator.

p: Effective population size (Ne) is the size of an ideal population that would show the same amount of random change in allele frequencies (genetic drift) as the real one.
When one sex has far fewer breeders, those few individuals give half of the genes to the next generation. So Ne ends up much lower than the head count.

x1C_160.eli: A class project with 10 kids and 90 kids pitching in may sound like 100 workers. But if only 10 of them decide the topic, the class has fewer real voices than it looks.
mem: Ne = 4(Nm)(Nf)/(Nm + Nf).
Unequal sex ratio makes Ne smaller than the census count.
Smaller Ne means stronger genetic drift.

fm.f: Ne = 4 x Nm x Nf / (Nm + Nf), where Nm = number of breeding males, Nf = number of breeding females, Ne = effective population size
fm.why: The question gives this formula, and it handles unequal numbers of males and females.
fm.nc: Do 4 x 10 = 40, then 40 x 90 = 3600. Divide by 100 by moving the decimal two places.

x1C_160.sc: Ne is always at or below the census count. Only 36 is below 100 and fits the formula.
x1C_160.trap: Averaging or adding the two sexes instead of using the product in the formula.
